title: Harness Dissection
subject: agent harnesses as a category
canonicalTask: Create a file called fizzbuzz.js that prints FizzBuzz for 1..20, then run it with node and show me the output.

copy.standfirst: Build a transferable model of agent harnesses as a category by dissecting DeepSeek Harness — then test whether that model explains a harness it was never derived from.

claims.title: You can't read what you can't name
claims.body: Writing a harness first supplies the vocabulary that makes a real one legible. Reading agent-loop cold teaches nothing; reading it after writing a loop teaches everything.

claims.title: The wire beats the source
claims.body: Prompt assembly is scattered across dozens of files. The bytes sent to the API are single, literal ground truth. When a reading and a capture disagree, the capture wins.

claims.title: A vocabulary must transfer
claims.body: Concepts that only explain their own specimen are worthless. The study succeeds if ideas derived from dsh explain Claude Code — and fails if they don't.

standingOrders.title: The canonical task
standingOrders.body: Used verbatim for every harness so captures stay comparable — your toy, dsh, and Claude Code all get the same prompt: {{canonicalTask}} It forces read, write, and execute in one run.

standingOrders.title: The surprise budget
standingOrders.body: There is no completion criterion. Abandon a thread after two consecutive findings that don't surprise you, and file it as a needs-triage issue. A dry thread is a result, not a failure.

standingOrders.title: The wire wins
standingOrders.body: When your reading of the source and the captured bytes disagree, the reading is wrong. Fix the note, not the capture.

standingOrders.title: Never commit captures
standingOrders.body: captures/ is gitignored and the proxy redacts auth headers before writing. A leaked key in a capture is the one unrecoverable mistake here.

standingOrders.title: Analyse, don't dump
standingOrders.body: dsh's prompt ships in a public MIT repo and can be quoted freely. Claude Code transcripts are personal working history — cite structure, counts, and tool names only. This repo is public.

standingOrders.title: Glossary as you go
standingOrders.body: When a thread sharpens a term, it lands in CONTEXT.md that session — never batched to the end. Terms get re-sorted in Phase 4, and being wrong early is data.

sections.s1: A language model is a function from text to text. It cannot read a file, run a command, or remember anything. A harness is the program wrapped around it that supplies all three. Everything else — compaction, permissions, plugins, sandboxing, delegation — is a refinement of one of these five steps, which is why §4 files each of the fifteen threads under the step it explains.
sections.s4: Lettered because there is no correct order, and grouped by which step of the loop each one explains — read a band top to bottom and you have one step fully accounted for. Each card carries the shortcut in your own harness that raised it (FROM), the packages it covers, and the command that opens it.
sections.s5: §4 is a filing system. This is the generating one. Phase 1's toy harness is not a warm-up, it is the question generator: every shortcut it takes is a question a real harness had to answer, and thirteen of the fifteen threads start life as a row in this table. Reading it top to bottom gives the order the study actually discovers things in — C, D, B, A, G, F, I, E, H, K, L, J, O.
sections.s6: Claude Code here runs on a subscription, so it's studied through the ~3,800 session transcripts already on disk rather than through wire capture. Know these limits before predicting against it.

map.lede: 0 → 1 → 2.0 is a strict chain; everything after it fans out. The fifteen threads have no order among themselves — but two things downstream are gated, and one of them is gated on a finding, not a phase. The five columns are the five steps of the loop above; click one to jump to its band.

loopSteps.label: Assemble
loopSteps.question: What goes into the request, and what gets left out?

loopSteps.label: Call
loopSteps.question: What sits between the harness and any model provider?

loopSteps.label: Execute
loopSteps.question: What the model asked for — and what is allowed to happen as a result.

loopSteps.label: Control
loopSteps.question: What makes it go round again — and what survives when it stops.

loopSteps.label: Around
loopSteps.question: The frame the loop sits in — none of these is a step, and that is the point.

phases.title: Pin the checkout
phases.body: Clone, detach at 47f9438, install frozen, build. Then discover and record the base-URL override and the non-interactive run command.
phases.pre: # pin the specimen git clone https://github.com/deepseek-ai/deepseek-harness.git \ ../deepseek-harness git -C ../deepseek-harness checkout 47f943859bef60e4160492346772ded9b24f765a # build it cd ../deepseek-harness && corepack enable pnpm install --frozen-lockfile && pnpm build # find the base-URL override — this is what lets you capture later rg -n 'baseURL|baseUrl|base_url|BASE_URL' packages/llm/ apps/ --type ts

phases.title: Build the capture proxy
phases.body: ~70 lines of dependency-free Node. Tees SSE to disk without buffering the client's view, and redacts authorization, x-api-key, api-key, cookie before any write.

halt.title: The one check you must not skip
halt.pre: rg -n 'sk-|Bearer' captures/session-smoke.jsonl # must print nothing
halt.body: A leaked key in a capture is the single unrecoverable mistake in this study. If that prints anything, stop and fix redact() before going further.

detail: Deliverables: .gitignore, tools/capture-proxy/server.mjs, and notes/00-orientation.md holding the pinned SHA, the package map, and the two discovered values every later task consumes by name.

phases.title: Write a harness from scratch
phases.body: ~45 lines against the DeepSeek API: a message list, two tools, a loop, a step cap. The only harness whose every byte you can account for — and therefore the reference against which dsh's captures are read.
phases.pre: messages = [system, user] for step in 1..10: msg = POST /chat/completions {model, messages, tools} messages.push(msg) if not msg.tool_calls: print(msg.content); break for call in msg.tool_calls: result = impls[call.name](call.args) messages.push({role:'tool', tool_call_id, content: result.slice(0,4000)})
detail: Then break it deliberately:

bullets: Blow the truncation — read package-lock.json and list the dependencies.
Blow the step cap — twelve sorting algorithms, each run and compared.
Expose the missing permission layer — delete every .tmp under /tmp. The alarm you feel is packages/guard's entire reason to exist.

detail: Deliverables: experiments/minimal-harness/harness.mjs, a capture of your own harness through the proxy, and notes/01-what-my-harness-lacks.md — the table that becomes §4 and §5. First real CONTEXT.md terms land here: loop, turn, step, tool call, tool result, context window.

phases.title: Baseline capture of dsh
phases.body: Capture dsh on the canonical task, then write notes/02-baseline-behavior.md recording only what was observable: round-trip count, tool order, when approval was requested, what displayed between steps, whether it verified its own work.
phases.pre: rg -n 'packages/' notes/02-baseline-behavior.md # must print nothing
detail: That note is the control Thread B must later reconcile against, line by line. It only works if it was written before you read any source.
Then diff your toy against the specimen: same task, two harnesses, two captures. Every difference is a thread to pull.

phases.title: One tool, two harnesses
phases.body: The same trivial tool built twice — as a dsh plugin and as an MCP server for Claude Code. The diff between the two integrations is the finding.
detail: Two things must be true, per harness: the tool was offered, and the model called it. Proving only the first is the classic false pass — it shows registration worked while the loop never closed around it.

detail.pre: # offered (dsh, from the capture) jq -r 'select(.dir=="request") | .body.tools[]? | .function.name' \ captures/session-plugin.jsonl | sort -u | rg hello_study # called (either harness — grep the marker) rg -c 'STUDY-MARKER-7f3a' captures/session-plugin.jsonl

detail: Why this is the category exam: what both harnesses demand of a tool is essential to the category. What only one demands is incidental to its implementation. That intersection is the real model of “a tool” — and MCP versus a Cordis plugin is itself an answer to Thread E's question about where an extension boundary belongs.
phases.note: — it does not wait for the other fourteen
phases.consumes: D's “what a new tool must provide” checklist

phases.title: Transfer test
phases.body: Commit predictions before opening the Claude Code transcripts already on disk, then score them. Sort every glossary term into universal, dsh-specific, or missing.
detail: Predict first, and commit the prediction. From the dsh-derived model alone, write down which tools you expect, how results appear serialized, what stop reasons exist, how permissions are gated. A prediction made after looking tests nothing — so it goes in a commit before the first jq runs.
Three buckets, and two of them are the output:

bullets: Universal — explains both harnesses. Stays canonical in CONTEXT.md.
dsh-specific — an implementation detail you mistook for a category concept.
Missing — Claude Code does something your vocabulary can't name. thinking blocks, hooks, and sidechains are the likely candidates.

detail: Buckets two and three are what the study actually produced. Bucket one is just what survived.
phases.note: · see §6 for what transcripts can and can't show

threads.name: Prompt & presentation
threads.question: What actually belongs in a system prompt, and how much behaviour is bought with prose rather than code?
detail: Answer with a number. What fraction of behavioural instruction lives in tool descriptions versus the system prompt? That ratio is a category-level property you can carry to any harness.
Take a distinctive six-word phrase from the capture and rg for it. If it isn't found literally, the prompt is assembled from fragments — record which, and where.

threads.name: The agent loop
threads.question: What legitimately terminates a loop? Your toy just used a hard step cap of ten.
threads.entry:
rg -n 'break|return|maxSteps|maxTurns|stop|finish' \
  packages/core/agent-loop --type ts
pnpm vitest run packages/core/agent-loop --reporter=verbose
detail: Mark the line where each of the five phases happens, then record every termination condition in precedence order — no tool calls emitted, step cap, token budget, user interrupt.

The tests are executable spec: an invariant you wouldn't have predicted marks a gap in your model. Then reconcile every observation in notes/02-baseline-behavior.md against a specific line, or list it as open — which is why this one waits for Task 2.0.

threads.name: Context & compaction
threads.question: What should be dropped when the context fills, and is the decision positional, semantic, or size-based?
detail: A monotonic rise followed by a drop in message count is a compaction event. The canonical task is too short to trigger one — run the twelve-algorithm task instead.
The densest engineering in the repo: compaction is a top-level package with a dedicated compaction-tool-result-pruner, and spill sits alongside it. Direct answer to your toy's worst shortcut.

threads.name: Tools & permission
threads.question: What must a harness be told about a tool, and where does the permission boundary sit?
detail: Trace the file-edit tool through six layers, each cited path:line: schema → registration → presentation → dispatch → permission → result serialization.

Then answer: is approval per-call, per-tool, per-session, or path-scoped — and what's the default posture? Output is a harness-neutral checklist, “what a new tool must provide,” which Phase 3 consumes directly.

threads.name: Plugin architecture
threads.question: Where should a harness's extension boundary sit, and what does “everything is a plugin” make hard?
threads.entry:
cat packages/core/README.md AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md packages/AGENTS.md
rg -n 'ctx\.(plugin|on|set|inject)' packages/core --type ts
detail: Learn Cordis first or this thread fails. It's dependency injection plus an event bus — nothing calls anything directly, so grep-based tracing finds nothing and the codebase reads as indirection with no call graph. There's a paper behind it: A Programming Paradigm for Spatiotemporal Composability.
The repo's own AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md are written to orient agents working in it, which makes them the best human onboarding docs too — usually fresher than docs/.

threads.name: Delegation & sub-agents
threads.question: When does a harness spawn another harness, and what does the child inherit?
detail: The design question is what a child inherits — tools? history? permissions? — and how its result re-enters the parent's context.
One of the sharpest comparison surfaces in the study. Claude Code has the same feature: sub-agent invocations appear in transcripts as Task/Agent tool calls, and isSidechain marks the child sessions.

threads.name: Execution & sandboxing
threads.question: Where does model-authored code actually run, and what contains it?
detail: Six packages here against your toy's bare execSync — that alone says the answer isn't obvious. Distinguish the layers: is code-runtime the abstraction, sandbox the local implementation, e2b a remote provider?

Then find the escape hatch — is there a path where code runs unsandboxed, and what gates it? Map the isolation strategies (none / subprocess / container / remote VM) and what each costs in latency and fidelity.

threads.name: Interop · MCP & ACP
threads.question: When a harness standardises its extension boundary, what does it give up?
threads.entry: cat packages/acp/README.md # Agent Client Protocol — what connects to what?
detail: Thread E covers the native extension boundary. This covers the standard one — and both harnesses under study speak MCP, making it the one integration surface you can compare directly.
The question that matters: which capabilities can a native plugin express that an MCP server cannot? That gap is precisely why native plugin systems still exist alongside MCP.

threads.name: Persistence & resumption
threads.question: What must be saved for a harness to resume a conversation it isn't currently holding in memory?
threads.entry:
rg -n 'persist|save|write|serialize' packages/session --type ts

F=$(find ~/.claude/projects -name '*.jsonl' | head -1)
jq -r '.type' "$F" | sort | uniq -c
detail: Your toy loses everything on exit. This is the thread with the richest comparison data, because Claude Code's own answer is sitting on your disk in ~3,800 files.
Then determine what session-query is for: is history searchable, and does the model get to search it, or only the user? That distinction is a real design fork.

threads.name: Observability & cost
threads.question: How does a harness let someone outside the loop observe it — or interrupt it?
detail: Map the hook points: which loop phases can be intercepted, and can a hook block an action or only observe it? In Claude Code the answer is visible — preventedContinuation on system records proves hooks there can block.
token-meter connects straight back to Thread C: does the harness count tokens before sending (budgeting) or after (accounting)? That determines whether compaction can be predictive.

threads.name: The host boundary
threads.question: Where does the harness end and the user interface begin? Could you drive it with no UI at all?
detail: Your toy printed to stdout. dsh serves a web UI on 127.0.0.1:3080, so it has drawn a boundary somewhere — and where that line sits determines whether the harness can be embedded, scripted, or driven headlessly.

Determine the transport between core and UI (HTTP, WebSocket, JSON-RPC, in-process?), and whether streaming reaches the UI as the raw model stream or as re-emitted domain events. Then answer the real question: what is the minimum surface a headless embedder needs?

threads.name: Provider abstraction
threads.question: What does it take to be model-agnostic, and where does the abstraction leak?
detail: Read the shared llm interface, then both implementations behind it. What sits in the interface that only one provider actually needs? That is where the abstraction leaks.
Then llm-retry: which failures are retried, with what backoff, and is a retried call visible to the loop or hidden beneath it? A hidden retry changes what “one step” means.
The category question: can a harness be genuinely model-agnostic, given that prompt engineering, tool-call formats, and thinking blocks all differ per model?

threads.name: Inputs & code intelligence
threads.question: What does a harness feed the model besides text and tool results?

raisedBy.text: the package census — the toy never raised this one

detail: attachment: how are images and files injected — re-sent every turn, or referenced? That has a direct cost consequence; connect it to Thread C.

lsp: the harness runs a language server and hands the model its output. Determine whether that arrives as a tool the model calls, or as context injected without being asked. Those are very different designs — decide which is better, and why dsh chose as it did.

threads.name: Cross-language embedding
threads.question: Can a TypeScript harness be driven from Python, and what does that boundary force it to make explicit?

raisedBy.text: the package census — the toy never raised this one

detail: An RPC boundary forces the cleanest possible statement of what a harness is, because everything crossing it must be serialisable. BENCHMARK.md points at a Python SDK and a jsonrpc-agent variant.

Read the SDK's surface — that operation list is dsh's own answer to “what is the harness API?” Then compare it to your toy's function signatures: what did dsh have to make explicit that you left implicit?

threads.name: Agent self-management
threads.question: What tools does a harness give the model for managing its own process, rather than the user's task?
detail: A category of tool your toy has no concept of: the model tracking its own plan, loading its own instructions, running predefined procedures. Every one has a direct Claude Code analogue, making this the densest comparison surface in the study.

bullets: todo — is the list context (re-sent every turn, costing tokens) or external state (stored, referenced)? That choice is the whole design question.
skill — does the model request one by name, or does the harness inject it on a match?
workflow — what distinguishes it from a plan (Thread F) and from a skill? If the code doesn't make that clear, the ambiguity is the finding.
